summary:
Fifteen verses from "the elder" to a man named Gaius, and one of the most concrete windows we have into everyday early church life. No doctrine is argued here. The subject is a local conflict over hospitality: which traveling missionaries a congregation will house, feed, and send on their way, and who gets to decide.

Three named men carry the story. Gaius is praised for supporting the traveling teachers, even when they were strangers to him; the elder tells him, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth" (v. 4). Diotrephes, "who loves to be first" (v. 9), refuses to receive the elder's messengers, spreads malicious talk about him, and expels members who dare to host the visitors. Demetrius, likely the letter's carrier, is commended as trustworthy. In effect the letter is a recommendation and a quiet counter-move: keep doing what you are doing, receive Demetrius, and do not imitate what is evil.

The value of 3 John is its realism. Generosity, ambition, gatekeeping, and the question of whom to trust were church problems from the beginning, handled through relationships rather than treatises — the elder closes by saying he would rather not use pen and ink, and hopes to talk face to face.
